title: A datacenter the world can live with
intro: Every requirement below is already met by a real site or written into a real rule somewhere in this ledger, with the document that proves it. Nothing here is a wish. The standard is the sum of practices that exist today, assembled in one place so that any site can be measured as a distance from it rather than judged as a sin. Where a requirement is met by a rule rather than a site, the rule is cited; where the record shows the practice but not yet the measured result, that is said.
how_to_read: Each requirement names what to ask for, what counts as proof, and which entry in the ledger shows it being done. 'Proof' always means a document someone outside the operator produced or assured.

requirements.title: Disclose site-level power and water, metered, every year
requirements.ask: Annual metered electricity (MWh) and water withdrawal, consumption and discharge (m³) for each site, published by the operator and reported to a public register.
requirements.proof: A statutory register or a settlement that binds future disclosure. A sustainability report alone is a claim.
requirements.note: The EU register exists and Germany's law mandates reporting; only 36% of in-scope EU sites reported in the first period. The Dalles settlement binds one operator at one site to annual disclosure. The rule is written; the practice is not yet general.

requirements.title: No drinking water for cooling where water is scarce; closed-loop or air cooling by default
requirements.ask: Cooling design stated in the permit, with the water source and the basin's status. In a stressed basin, air or closed-loop cooling. Where water is plentiful, seawater or reuse water before potable.
requirements.proof: The environmental assessment or permit naming the cooling system and the daily volume; a utility stating the connection is for office use only.
requirements.note: Uruguay's redesign cut stated operational water from 7,600 to 48 m³ a day. Hamina cools with seawater. Amsterdam prohibits groundwater extraction. Noord-Holland's water company now connects datacenters for office use only. These are permits and policies, not promises.

requirements.title: Waste heat goes into a heat network, and the delivered figure is published
requirements.ask: Connection to a district heating system where one exists or can be built, with delivered MWh published by the network operator. Where no network exists, a cost-benefit analysis on the public record explaining why.
requirements.proof: The heat utility's annual report or a public body's case study giving delivered MWh; a statute requiring the analysis.
requirements.note: Stockholm's half-municipal utility reports 117 GWh of recovered heat in its statutory accounts. Tallaght's council-owned network publishes cumulative MWh and tonnes. Denmark now requires every datacenter above 1 MW to analyse and use surplus heat unless infeasible; Germany sets 10% reuse rising to 20%. Across the EU the first reporting period found 1.8% of heat reused, so the gap between the rule and the practice is the distance to close.

requirements.title: Firm, additional, clean supply, or bring your own
requirements.ask: Electricity from a contracted clean source that would not otherwise have been built (geothermal, hydro allocation, existing nuclear restructured to pay grid charges), or the obligation to bring dispatchable supply before connecting. Annual renewable certificates do not meet this.
requirements.proof: A regulator-approved tariff or supply agreement naming the resource; a connection policy that requires it.
requirements.note: Nevada's regulator approved firm geothermal for a datacenter under a tariff stated not to shift cost to other customers. Ireland requires new sites to bring dispatchable capacity equal to their import and to source 80% from new Irish renewables. Quebec allocates hydro and scores projects on heat recovery. What none of these yet has on the public record is hourly matching verified by a third party; that is the next bar.

requirements.title: No new fossil generation built for the site, and no unpermitted generation ever
requirements.ask: The interconnection and utility filings show the load is served without a new gas plant built for it. On-site generators are permitted before they run, sized and listed in the air permit.
requirements.proof: The grid operator's queue and the utility commission's order; the air permit with generator count and capacity.
requirements.note: Ireland's planning board refused a site because on-site gas could become its primary supply; its regulator states islanded gas datacenters are inconsistent with national policy. A Dutch court upheld the grid operator's right to pause connections rather than overbuild. The counter-examples in the ledger (a 944 MW peaker in Virginia, turbines run for a year before permitting in Memphis, 4,678 MW of gas in Pennsylvania) are what this requirement is measured against.

requirements.title: The site pays for the grid it needs
requirements.ask: Large loads pay for the transmission and generation built to serve them, with a minimum-take obligation and a long contract, so that residential bills do not carry the cost.
requirements.proof: A utility commission order setting the tariff; an auditor's or market monitor's finding of the bill effect.
requirements.note: Ohio requires loads above 25 MW to pay for 85% of subscribed capacity for up to 12 years. Ontario wrote cost responsibility into statute. The PJM market monitor's $16.6 billion and Virginia's auditor's $14–37 a month are the measure of what happens without such rules.

requirements.title: Land take is accounted for and biodiversity is a condition, not a brochure
requirements.ask: Hectares taken and previous land use stated in the application; a biodiversity condition with a metric, a monitoring duty and an enforcement body; siting rules that keep hyperscale off farmland and out of green belts unless a public body decides otherwise in writing.
requirements.proof: A planning decision with the condition in it; a national siting rule.
requirements.note: England's Secretary of State imposed an enforceable 135% biodiversity net gain condition. The Netherlands confined hyperscale siting to two named areas by decree and the state refused to sell the Zeewolde land. Monitoring data from the English site does not exist yet because it is not built; the condition is the proof, the result is pending.

requirements.title: Noise is measured by a third party, before and after, and the results are public
requirements.ask: A baseline sound study before construction, a post-construction study, and annual studies for five years, all by an independent firm, with a design requirement that site noise not exceed ambient; a limit that addresses low-frequency tonal noise, which dBA does not capture.
requirements.proof: The ordinance or planning condition; the published studies.
requirements.note: Chandler, Arizona wrote the studies into its ordinance. No city has yet published the results, and no ordinance in the ledger addresses tonal noise, which is what residents actually complain about. This requirement is half-proven.

requirements.title: Public money buys audited jobs, with a clawback
requirements.ask: Any tax exemption or subsidy names the permanent on-site jobs and wages required, is evaluated by an independent auditor on a schedule, and is clawed back if the terms are not met.
requirements.proof: The incentive agreement; the auditor's evaluation.
requirements.note: Georgia and Virginia at least evaluate their exemptions by law, which is how Georgia's 70% overcount came to light. No programme in the ledger ties the money to a jobs floor with a clawback. This requirement is proven only in its first half: the audit exists; the condition does not.

requirements.title: Hardware lives as long as it can, and the reuse figure is assured
requirements.ask: Stated hardware lifespans, a reuse and recovery rate for servers and components, and the mineral sourcing for cobalt, nickel and rare earths traced to the mine, all within a third-party assurance scope.
requirements.proof: An assurance statement whose scope names the figure.
requirements.note: Microsoft publishes a 90.9% reuse rate and a method for it; the assurance scope covers waste tonnage, not that rate. No company in the ledger has an assured hardware reuse figure, and statutory conflict-minerals filings do not cover cobalt, nickel or rare earths. This is the least-met requirement in the standard.

requirements.title: The grid operator publishes a reconciled datacenter forecast
requirements.ask: Queued, contracted and actually connected datacenter load published separately and reconciled, so that planning is not done against announcements.
requirements.proof: The grid operator's own forecast document.
requirements.note: Australia's AEMO publishes a project-reconciled forecast showing 67 GW in development, 27% connection utilisation and a 36% cancellation rate. Spain's grid operator maps granted and requested access by type. Ireland's statistics office meters the share. Texas, by contrast, publishes no file of its 445 GW queue.

requirements.title: The mines and fabs behind the hardware move off inland water
requirements.ask: Copper, lithium and chip fabrication report water by source, with inland withdrawal falling and seawater or reuse rising, in regulator-published figures.
requirements.proof: The mining or water regulator's data, not the company's report.
requirements.note: Chile's copper regulator records inland water use falling in absolute terms as desalination grows to two thirds of supply by 2034. That is one mineral in one country; the same figure does not exist for nickel in Indonesia or rare earths in Myanmar.

closing: Twelve requirements. Each is met somewhere. None is met everywhere, and three (noise results, jobs clawbacks, assured hardware reuse) are met only in part anywhere. A site that meets all twelve does not exist yet, and nothing in the record says it cannot.
